name: Skin bleaching injections (glutathione IV)

lead: Glutathione is an antioxidant the body makes. Some clinics sell it as intravenous whitening drips, promoted to lighten skin and clear undertones, and Wikipedia describes it as the most common agent taken by mouth to whiten skin. The payoff people want is a lighter, more even skin tone.

It is said to inhibit tyrosinase and shift melanin production toward lighter pigment. A 2016 review in the Indian Journal of Dermatology, Venereology and Leprology concluded that no evidence proves IV glutathione works for skin lightening, and Wikipedia says it is unclear whether glutathione works. In looksmaxxing communities it is sometimes discussed as a way to lighten skin tone or undertones.

paras: It is offered in clinics and spas as a series of IV sessions, alongside oral and topical glutathione products. Any change in tone is described as gradual, with repeat sessions marketed to keep it.

The Philippine drug regulator issued a warning against IV use after adverse effects, and the Philippine government advises against it. The 2016 review found evidence for safety and efficacy limited. People with pigment concerns can ask a dermatologist about options.

web.title: PubMed search results: glutathione skin lightening randomized placebo

angle.text: IV glutathione is sold as a whitening drip, promoted to reduce melanin and give a lighter, more even skin tone. A 2016 review found no evidence proving it lightens skin, and a regulator has warned against IV use.

lead: Glutathione is a small antioxidant molecule, a tripeptide made naturally by the body. It is promoted, in oral, topical and intravenous (IV) forms, as a skin-lightening agent, and IV or injected versions are sometimes sold as "whitening drips".[1][2] People who use it are generally aiming for a lighter overall skin tone, more even complexion or clearer undertone. Wikipedia describes glutathione as the most common agent taken by mouth to whiten skin.[2]

The proposed route to a lighter look is biochemical: a 2016 review in the Indian Journal of Dermatology, Venereology and Leprology says the lightening effect is attributed to direct and indirect inhibition of the enzyme tyrosinase and a shift from dark eumelanin to lighter phaeomelanin production.[1] The same review states that there is a dichotomy between the evidence for efficacy and for safety, that no evidence proves IV glutathione works for skin lightening, that the hype around its depigmentary properties may be a marketing matter, and that adverse effects from IV use led the Philippine drug regulator to issue a warning.[1] Wikipedia likewise says it is unclear whether glutathione works and notes that the Philippine government advises against IV use.[2]

In looksmaxxing communities it is sometimes discussed as a way to lighten skin tone or undertones. In strength-training forums, injectable glutathione also comes up as a wellness add-on that some doctors prescribe alongside testosterone therapy.[3][4]
infobox: Lighter skin tone via reduced melanin production[1]
Philippine authorities warn against IV use[1][2]

paras: The review states that glutathione's lightening effect is attributed to direct and indirect inhibition of the enzyme tyrosinase, which controls melanin synthesis, and to a shift from eumelanin (dark pigment) to phaeomelanin (lighter pigment) production.[1] It describes glutathione as a thiol-tripeptide with a prominent role in maintaining intracellular redox balance and notes that the discovery of its antimelanogenic properties led to its promotion as a skin-lightening agent.[1]

Wikipedia's glutathione article states that the systemic availability of orally administered glutathione is poor, attributing this to breakdown by digestive proteases and to the lack of a specific glutathione carrier in cell membranes, and mentions that N-acetylcysteine, a cysteine precursor, helps replenish intracellular glutathione.[5] The poor oral availability is the usual explanation given for why injections or drips are marketed for lightening rather than capsules.[5] A forum member discussing NAC describes it as a precursor to glutathione.[6]

The 2016 review found a gap between how widely IV glutathione is used and the evidence supporting it, stating that no evidence proves efficacy for skin lightening and raising the possibility that its promotion is commercially driven.[1] Wikipedia says whether glutathione works remains unclear as of 2019 and lists it among whiteners that may contain harmful ingredients.[2]

The Philippine government recommends against intravenous use because of possible side effects, according to Wikipedia.[2] Other skin-lightening agents covered on the same page carry documented risks: mercury compounds, linked to neurological and kidney problems; hydroquinone, associated with ochronosis and cataracts in long-term use; and potent topical corticosteroids, which can cause skin atrophy over time.[2] Lightened skin is also reported to be more vulnerable to sun damage and infection.[2]

Proponents of whitening drips argue that intravenous delivery bypasses poor oral absorption and produces a stronger effect than capsules; the 2016 review notes that IV use has outpaced the evidence for it.[1][5] Oral and topical glutathione have more published trial data than IV use, as summarized under Clinical studies.[7]

Skin lightening is widespread in parts of Asia, Africa and elsewhere, and glutathione is among the products used.[2] Wikipedia cites 2013 survey figures of about 77 percent of Nigerian women, 52 percent of Senegalese women and 25 percent of Malian women using lightening products, and reports that in India more than half of skin-care sales are lightening products.[2] The European Union banned hydroquinone from cosmetics in 2000, and many countries prohibit mercury compounds in skin products.[2]

A forum thread on looksmax.org asks whether glutathione injections clear skin undertones, with one poster reporting that their eyes looked lighter after a first IV session. In T Nation threads, glutathione injections appear in lists of wellness add-ons that a user says were prescribed by a TRT doctor or used alongside testosterone, and one participant suggests intravenous glutathione after reading about detox, without recommending it.[3][4][8]

No studies found establishing efficacy of IV glutathione for skin lightening; the 2016 review states that no evidence proves it.[1] Registered trials involving glutathione concern other conditions, such as a 30-patient phase 2 trial in gingival hyperpigmentation that also lists vitamin C, and trials of glutathione-related compounds in cancers, liver failure, type 1 diabetes and autism.[9][10][11][12] A 2018 case report described intravenous glutathione used with conventional therapy in a patient with Parkinson's disease.[13]

Research on non-IV glutathione is larger. The 2016 review cites three randomized controlled trials supporting a skin-lightening effect and good safety for topical and oral glutathione, while raising open questions about treatment duration and how long any lightening lasts.[7] Published randomized trials include a 2012 double-blind placebo-controlled study of oral glutathione at 500 mg/day for four weeks, measuring skin melanin index and UV spots; a 2021 trial of combined topical and oral glutathione applied to each side of the face, which reported a statistically significant difference in the L* (lightness) score; a 2021 Indonesian multicentre trial of an oral glutathione supplement combined with ascorbic acid, alpha-lipoic acid and zinc aspartate over 12 weeks, whose authors said more research was needed; and a 2022 trial of oral L-cystine with reduced glutathione in women.[7]

Systematic reviews include a 2019 review in the Journal of Cosmetic Dermatology reporting a trend that glutathione might brighten skin in sun-exposed areas, and a 2025 review in the International Journal of Dermatology on glutathione for skin lightening and melasma.[7] These concern oral and topical products; the 2016 review states that no evidence proves the intravenous route is effective.[1]

lore.intro: On looksmax.org, glutathione IV is discussed as a possible way to lighten skin tone or clear undertones. In lifting forums it appears mainly as an adjunct supplement or injectable.[3][4]
